conditions: ABCD is a tetrahedron, hence vertices are distinct.
The three vectors start at A.
A is the coordinate origin; b=AB,c=AC,d=AD.
view_solutions.independent_solution: DB=b-d, CD=d-c and BC=c-b. Their opposites from A are AX=d-b, AY=c-d, AZ=b-c. This is precisely the complete row B. Each edge is nonzero; reversing any one required expression changes the vector.

option_checks.evidence: The row gives (b-d,d-c,c-b), the original DB,CD,BC directions instead of their opposites. All three components are reversed relative to the target.
Each listed difference is the negative of the requested directed edge: -(b-d)=d-b, -(d-c)=c-d, -(c-b)=b-c. A is the tail of each displayed output.
AX and AZ agree, but AY=d-c is CD, not -CD=c-d. Equality of these opposite expressions would require c=d, impossible for a tetrahedron.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same tetrahedron, AY is (0,-1,1), whereas the required AY is (0,1,-1).

option_checks.evidence: AX and AY agree, but AZ=c-b is BC, not -BC=b-c. Equality would require b=c, impossible here.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same tetrahedron, AZ is (-1,1,0), whereas the required AZ is (1,-1,0).

task_fidelity.evidence: The complete reversed-vector triple preserves all three sources, the tail A and each ordered sign. Distinguishing enough components is legitimate elimination; no source task is reduced to an exposed numeric cell.
capacity_losses: Independent drawing and translation to A.

redundancy.evidence: All four triples are different under tetrahedron nondegeneracy. C isolates the middle reversal and D the last; A reverses all three. A subset of component comparisons can eliminate rows, but a correct full row is the response unit.

conditions: O,A,B are noncollinear, so a,b are linearly independent.
O is the common origin, not A.
c=OC=a-b.
Boundary order is O-B-A-C-O.
view_solutions.independent_solution: OB=b, BA=a-b, AC=c-a=-b, CO=-c=b-a. The complete tuple is (b,a-b,-b,b-a), row D. The opposite boundary vectors cancel: OB=-AC and BA=-CO. Equivalently OB=CA and BA=OC, the sufficient opposite-side relations for nondegenerate parallelogram OBAC. Independence of a,b ensures the figure is not collinear.

option_checks.evidence: OB=b and AC=-b agree. BA is b-a instead of a-b, and CO is a-b instead of b-a. Both are reversed; a=b would be required to remove the error.
OB and BA agree, but AC is b instead of -b, and CO is a-b instead of b-a. The whole path would sum to 2a, not zero. Noncollinearity excludes a=0 and b=0.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same noncollinear O,A,B, AC is (0,1) rather than (0,-1), and CO is (1,-1) rather than (-1,1).

option_checks.evidence: The first vector OB is a instead of b; BA is reversed; AC is -a instead of -b; CO is reversed. Independence of a,b excludes equality of either swapped expression.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same noncollinear O,A,B, this row is ((1,0),(-1,1),(-1,0),(1,-1)), with none of its four components correct.

option_checks.evidence: The four expressions follow by ordered endpoint subtraction, and the first/third and second/fourth are opposite pairs. They produce the exact boundary order O-B-A-C-O.

task_fidelity.evidence: The correct tuple contains the sufficient equal-and-parallel opposite-side relationships, with noncollinearity and order intact. The view's task is the boundary tuple, not explicit production or narration of the parallelogram proof.
capacity_losses: Independent articulation of the inference from opposite boundary vectors to a parallelogram.
task_fidelity.claim_limit: Do not report this click as independently proving OBAC or independently naming its shape.

answer_leakage.evidence: The ordered path and OB=b define inputs rather than a marked output. fig-76 supplies O->A,O->B,A->B, not a complete rendered OBAC. That concept aid supports subtraction but does not supply the four-entry answer.

conditions: ABC is a nondegenerate triangle.
O lies outside plane ABC.
All outputs start at O.
P midpoint OA, R midpoint OB, M midpoint AC, N midpoint AB.
view_solutions.independent_solution: Take O as origin: a=OA,b=OB,c=OC, p=a/2,r=b/2,m=(a+c)/2,n=(a+b)/2. The targets are x=a-b,y=-a-c,z=a+b-c. Reflecting B in P gives 2p-b=a-b. Taking OY=-2OM gives y=-2m=-a-c. Reflecting C in N gives 2n-c=a+b-c. All three methods in row A are correct. The O-outside-plane condition makes a,b,c independent and preserves the spatial construction scope.

option_checks.evidence: X=2P-B=a-b; OY=-2OM=-a-c; Z=2N-C=a+b-c. Each described endpoint is exactly the endpoint of the required vector from O.
The X,Z constructions agree, but OY=2OM=a+c has the opposite sign to the required -a-c. Under the stated tetrahedral geometry a+c is nonzero.
Reflecting A in R gives X=2R-A=b-a, the reverse of a-b. Y,Z agree. A=B would be required to make the two X results coincide, contrary to the triangle premise.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same example required X=(1,-1,0), but the row gives X=(-1,1,0).

option_checks.evidence: X,Y agree. Reflecting N in C gives Z=2c-n, whereas reflecting C in N requires Z=2n-c. Their difference is 3(c-n), nonzero because nondegenerate triangle vertex C is not the midpoint of AB.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same example N=(1/2,1/2,0), so this row gives Z=(-1/2,-1/2,2) instead of (1,1,-1). Its coefficient sum is 1 as well: plane membership alone would not detect this wrong endpoint.

task_fidelity.evidence: All three operations survive, including -OA-OC, start O and the outside-plane condition. Reflection center/subject, midpoint factor and sign determine actual geometric endpoints. No arbitrary point click substitutes for these construction claims.
capacity_losses: Independent drawing and execution of the three constructions.
task_fidelity.scope_note: The correct X is in the plane through O parallel to ABC, Y is not in ABC, and Z is in ABC. These diagnostics were independently retained; explicit plane-membership testing was not demanded by source 188.

redundancy.evidence: Each wrong row alters a different construction component. Recognizing reflection algebra or eliminating mismatches still requires the mathematical relationships. D lies in the base plane too, so spatial scope is not a substitute for checking the endpoint.

answer_leakage.evidence: The named midpoints do not give the correct operations. Even if a learner uses ordinal 2 for the direction a-b, they must still distinguish -2OM from 2OM and the two reversed central reflections.

conditions: ABC is nondegenerate, so u=CA and v=CB are nonzero.
The angle is at C.
Each alternative is a universally valid conditional claim for such triangles.
view_solutions.independent_solution: |u+v|^2-|u-v|^2=4(u dot v). For nonzero u,v this is zero exactly when angle ACB is right. This proves both norm implications A and C. The vector equation in B would require v=0; equality of the individual lengths in D is not forced by orthogonality.

option_checks.evidence: At angle ACB=90 degrees, u dot v=0; both squared norms equal |u|^2+|v|^2, hence both norms are equal.
u+v=u-v implies 2v=0, impossible because B and C are distinct. A right-angle triangle exists, so the implication is not vacuously true.
option_checks.counterexample: C=(0,0),A=(1,0),B=(0,2): u+v=(1,2), u-v=(1,-2); these are distinct vectors although their norms are equal.

option_checks.evidence: Equality of the norms gives 4(u dot v)=0. Both nonzero vectors are perpendicular, so angle ACB=90 degrees. The nondegenerate triangle premise excludes zero-vector angle ambiguity.
The premise forces perpendicularity, not equal operand lengths. Unequal-leg right triangles satisfy the premise.

task_fidelity.evidence: Both source implications are explicitly tested. The false claims force norm/vector and equal-diagonal/equal-side distinctions. The triangle and angle vertex remain exact.

conditions: ABCD is a parallelogram in cyclic order.
M is the common midpoint of diagonals AC and BD.
O,P are arbitrary spatial points and may coincide.
Q defines arbitrary-origin sums, not a new geometric constraint.
view_solutions.independent_solution: For any Q, QA+QC=(a-q)+(c-q)=2(m-q)=2QM; QB+QD has the same value because b+d=2m. Thus S_O=T_O=2OM and S_P=T_P=2PM, row C. The factor two, direction and origin dependence all matter.

option_checks.evidence: Both rows omit the factor two. They coincide with the correct values only when the respective origin equals M, not for arbitrary origins.
The O value is correct, but the P sum must use PM, not OM. Equality 2PM=2OM requires P=O. An allowed coincident case cannot validate the universal statement.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same parallelogram and distinct O,P, the proposed P value is (0,0,-2), but the actual P sum is (0,0,-4).

option_checks.evidence: Each pair of opposite-vertex vectors sums to twice the vector from its own origin to the common diagonal midpoint. This is valid for all O,P, including coincident, in-plane or outside-plane cases.
MO=-OM and MP=-PM. The row reverses both correct sums; it can coincide only at the zero-vector midpoint special case, not universally.
option_checks.counterexample: For the same example, D proposes (0,0,2) and (0,0,4), opposite to the actual sums (0,0,-2) and (0,0,-4).

task_fidelity.evidence: The universal spatial origin and conditional parallelogram identity remain. The two-origin extension reveals dependence on each tail, and the common-value formula is a sufficient midpoint proof relationship.
capacity_losses: Independent written proof for all spatial O.

redundancy.evidence: A tests magnitude, B origin dependence, D direction. All three are false universal rows even though special choices can collapse their values; C alone works for arbitrary origins.

answer_leakage.evidence: The stem never asserts S_Q=T_Q or the correct midpoint value. Ordinal 3's alternatives use another local M and do not establish the arbitrary-origin opposite-pair identity.

conditions: Initial tetrahedron vertices are considered, followed by any four points.
The universal extension includes coplanar, collinear and coincident cases.
M midpoint AB and N midpoint CD exist also in degenerate cases.
p=AD+BC, q=BD+AC use the exact directed signs.
view_solutions.independent_solution: Using any common origin, p=(d-a)+(c-b)=c+d-a-b and q=(d-b)+(c-a)=c+d-a-b for every four points. Also 2MN=2(n-m)=c+d-a-b. Thus A and C are true. AB+CD=b-a+d-c differs from the common value by 2(b-c), so B is not universal. Since the identity holds for all points, a collinear counterexample in D does not exist.

option_checks.evidence: Both ordered sums reduce to c+d-a-b with no tetrahedral condition. This proves the tetrahedron case and all arbitrary-four-point cases.
AB+CD=b-a+d-c. Subtracting it from p=q gives 2(c-b), which is nonzero whenever B and C differ. Some coincident cases can make B true, but it is not true for any four points.
m=(a+b)/2 and n=(c+d)/2; 2MN=2(n-m)=c+d-a-b=p=q. The directed order M->N and factor two are essential, and the formula survives coincident points.
The universal identity p=q holds in particular for all collinear points, so the asserted existence of a collinear counterexample is false. A general algebraic proof refutes the existential claim.
option_checks.counterexample: Illustration, not the refutation's whole proof: on a line A=0,B=1,C=3,D=7, both sums are 9.

task_fidelity.evidence: The initial and unrestricted cases both survive. A tests the scope; C supplies an independent common-value relationship; B tests ordered-edge addition; D tests the unrestricted extension. No parallelogram assumption has been imported from ordinal 5.
capacity_losses: Independent written justification of scope without geometric restrictions.
